decks.title: Rectilinear Figures: Parallelograms — Part 1: Sides, angles and diagonals
goals: Use the equal opposite sides and angles and the 180 degree rule of a parallelogram
Prove that the opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, also from one equal and parallel pair of sides
Prove that the diagonals bisect each other and cut the parallelogram into two congruent triangles
Use these facts to find unknown sides, angles and lengths

slides.heading: Parallelograms, Part 1
slides.body_md: A **parallelogram** has both pairs of opposite sides **parallel**. In this part we find what that forces: equal sides, equal angles and **diagonals that bisect each other**.

visual.alt: Parallelogram A B C D. A B and D C carry the same single arrow mark and a single tick, so they are parallel and equal. A D and B C carry double arrow marks and double ticks, so they are parallel and equal.
visual.caption: Opposite sides are parallel (arrows) and equal (ticks).

slides.narration: Welcome. A parallelogram is a four sided figure with both pairs of opposite sides parallel. That one idea forces a lot. Opposite sides are equal, opposite angles are equal, and the diagonals cut each other in half. In this part we prove the important results and use them to find unknown angles and lengths.

slides.heading: What is a parallelogram?
slides.body_md:
A quadrilateral $ABCD$ is a **parallelogram** when $AB \parallel DC$ and $AD \parallel BC$.

The arrows in the figure mark the two parallel pairs.

visual.alt: Parallelogram A B C D with arrow marks showing that A B is parallel to D C and A D is parallel to B C.
visual.caption: A parallelogram has both pairs of opposite sides parallel.

slides.narration: A quadrilateral is a parallelogram when both pairs of opposite sides are parallel. In the figure the single arrows mark the pair A B and D C, and the double arrows mark the pair A D and B C. This is the definition. Everything else in this chapter is a consequence of it.

slides.heading: Sides of a parallelogram
slides.body_md:
The **opposite sides are equal**: $AB = DC$ and $AD = BC$.

In the figure $AB = DC = 8$ cm and $AD = BC = 4.5$ cm, so the perimeter is $2(8 + 4.5) = 25$ cm.

*The proof that both pairs of opposite sides are equal is not in the ICSE 2028 Class IX syllabus; we use the result.*

visual.alt: Parallelogram A B C D drawn to scale with A B equal to eight centimetres and A D equal to four point five centimetres. The opposite sides D C and B C carry the same tick marks, so they are equal to them.
visual.caption: Drawn to scale: A B = D C = 8 cm, A D = B C = 4.5 cm.

slides.narration: The opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal. In the figure A B and D C are each eight centimetres, and A D and B C are each four point five centimetres. So the perimeter is two times eight plus four point five, which is twenty five centimetres. The proof of this result is not required in the syllabus, so we simply use it.

slides.heading: Angles: neighbours add up to 180 degrees
slides.body_md: Since $AD \parallel BC$, the angles $\angle A$ and $\angle B$ are **co-interior angles** on the transversal $AB$, so $\angle A + \angle B = 180^\circ$.

rows: Opposite, such as A and C
Neighbouring, such as A and B

visual.alt: Table of the angle facts of a parallelogram: opposite angles are equal, neighbouring angles add up to one hundred eighty degrees and all four angles add up to three hundred sixty degrees.

slides.narration: Look at the angles at A and B. The sides A D and B C are parallel, and A B cuts across them. So the angles at A and B are co-interior angles, and they add up to one hundred eighty degrees. In the figure with angle A equal to sixty two, angle B is one hundred eighteen. Every pair of neighbouring angles in a parallelogram adds up to one hundred eighty degrees.

slides.heading: Theorem: opposite angles are equal
slides.body_md:
**Theorem.** The opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal.

In parallelogram $ABCD$: $\angle A = \angle C$ and $\angle B = \angle D$.

visual.alt: Parallelogram A B C D with angle A and angle C each sixty two degrees, shown with one arc, and angle B and angle D each one hundred eighteen degrees, shown with two arcs.
visual.caption: Opposite angles are equal; neighbouring angles add to 180 degrees.

slides.narration: Here is the theorem. In a parallelogram the opposite angles are equal. In the figure angle A and angle C are both sixty two degrees, shown with one arc, and angle B and angle D are both one hundred eighteen degrees, shown with two arcs. Notice that sixty two plus one hundred eighteen is one hundred eighty, as neighbouring angles must be. Now we prove it.

slides.heading: Proof that opposite angles are equal
slides.body_md: Use the co-interior angles twice. Both pairs of sides are parallel, so both give a sum of $180^\circ$.

rows: the same argument with $\angle C + \angle D = 180^\circ$

visual.alt: Table of four claims and reasons proving that the opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, using two pairs of co-interior angles.

slides.narration: The proof uses co-interior angles twice. A D is parallel to B C, with transversal A B, so angle A plus angle B is one hundred eighty degrees. A B is parallel to D C, with transversal B C, so angle B plus angle C is one hundred eighty degrees. Both sums equal one hundred eighty, so angle A equals angle C. The same argument gives angle B equal to angle D.

slides.heading: Quick check: which angles are equal?
slides.body_md: Pick the pair that must be equal in every parallelogram.

visual.alt: Parallelogram A B C D with angle A and angle C marked a, shown with one arc, and angle B marked b, shown with two arcs. The proof shows that a plus b is one hundred eighty.
visual.caption: Co-interior angles: a + b = 180, so the opposite angles are equal.

slides.narration: In a parallelogram A B C D, which pair of angles must be equal? Use the figure. The angles marked with one arc are equal, and the angle marked with two arcs is the supplement. Choose the pair that is equal in every parallelogram, not just in special ones.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: all the angles
slides.body_md: In parallelogram $PQRS$, $\angle P = 64^\circ$. Find $a = \angle Q$, $b = \angle R$ and $c = \angle S$.
bullets: **Step 2 —** $\angle R = \angle P = 64^\circ$ and $\angle S = \angle Q = 116^\circ$ (opposite angles).

visual.alt: Parallelogram P Q R S with angle P equal to sixty four degrees. The angles at Q, R and S are marked a, b and c.
visual.caption: Find a, b and c.

slides.narration: The angle at Q is next to the angle at P, so they add to one hundred eighty. Angle Q is one hundred sixteen degrees. The angle at R is opposite the angle at P, so it is sixty four degrees. The angle at S is opposite the angle at Q, so it is one hundred sixteen degrees. As a check, the four angles add up to three hundred sixty degrees.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: angles with x
slides.body_md: In parallelogram $ABCD$, $\angle A = (3x + 10)^\circ$ and $\angle B = (2x + 30)^\circ$. Find $x$ and the angles.

visual.alt: Table of five steps: the neighbouring angles three x plus ten and two x plus thirty add up to one hundred eighty, so x is twenty eight, angle A is ninety four and angle B is eighty six degrees.

slides.narration: The angles A and B are neighbours, so they add to one hundred eighty. Three x plus ten plus two x plus thirty equals one hundred eighty, which gives five x plus forty equals one hundred eighty. So x is twenty eight. Then angle A is ninety four degrees and angle B is eighty six degrees. Check that they add to one hundred eighty.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: sides with x
slides.body_md: In parallelogram $ABCD$, $AB = (2x + 3)$ cm, $DC = (5x - 12)$ cm and $AD = 8$ cm. Find $x$, $AB$ and the perimeter.

visual.alt: Parallelogram A B C D with A B equal to two x plus three centimetres, D C equal to five x minus twelve centimetres and A D equal to eight centimetres.
visual.caption: Opposite sides are equal: find x.

slides.narration: The opposite sides A B and D C are equal. So two x plus three equals five x minus twelve. That gives three x equals fifteen, and x is five. Then A B is thirteen centimetres. The sides A D and B C are eight each, so the perimeter is two times thirteen plus eight, which is forty two centimetres.

slides.heading: One pair equal and parallel
slides.body_md:
If $AB \parallel DC$ and $AB = DC$ in a quadrilateral $ABCD$, then $ABCD$ is a **parallelogram**.

*The proof of this test is not in the ICSE 2028 Class IX syllabus; we use it, and we prove the angle result that follows.*

visual.alt: Quadrilateral A B C D in which A B and D C carry the same arrow and the same tick, so they are parallel and equal.
visual.caption: One pair of opposite sides is equal and parallel.

slides.narration: Sometimes we are told less. Suppose in a quadrilateral A B C D, the side A B is parallel and equal to D C. Then A B C D is a parallelogram. The proof of this test is not part of the syllabus, so we use it. What the syllabus does ask is the next result: proving that the opposite angles are equal from this one pair.

slides.heading: Opposite angles from one equal parallel pair
slides.body_md: Join $AC$. The shaded triangles $ABC$ and $CDA$ have $AB = CD$, $AC$ in common, and equal alternate angles $\angle BAC = \angle DCA$.

rows: corresponding parts: alternate angles, so $AD \parallel BC$

visual.alt: Table of six claims and reasons for a quadrilateral with one pair of opposite sides equal and parallel: join the diagonal, prove the two triangles congruent, and add the angles at A and C to get angle A equal to angle C.

slides.narration: Join A to C. The triangles A B C and C D A match. A B equals C D, given. The angles B A C and D C A are alternate angles between the parallel lines, so they are equal. And A C is common. Two sides and the angle between them agree, so the triangles are congruent. Then angle B equals angle D. Adding the two parts at A and at C gives angle A equal to angle C.

slides.heading: The proof in the figure
slides.body_md: The alternate angles marked $p$ are equal because $AB \parallel DC$. The congruent triangles are shaded.

visual.alt: Quadrilateral A B C D in which A B is parallel and equal to D C. The diagonal A C is dashed. Triangles A B C and C D A are shaded. Angle B A C and angle D C A are alternate angles, both marked p.
visual.caption: Join A C: triangles A B C and C D A match.

slides.narration: In the figure the diagonal A C is dashed and the two triangles are shaded. The angles marked p are the alternate angles, equal because A B is parallel to D C. Once the triangles are congruent, the angles marked at B and at D are equal, and the angles of the triangles at A and at C add together to give equal angles A and C.

slides.heading: Quick check: neighbouring angles
slides.body_md: Decide whether Neha's report is possible.

rows: Opposite, such as A and C
Neighbouring, such as A and B

visual.alt: Table of the angle facts of a parallelogram: opposite angles are equal, neighbouring angles add up to one hundred eighty degrees and all four angles add up to three hundred sixty degrees.

slides.narration: Neha measures a parallelogram shaped ring frame and reports two neighbouring angles of seventy degrees and one hundred degrees. Is her report possible? Remember the rule for neighbouring angles of a parallelogram, and add the two numbers.

slides.heading: Diagonals bisect each other
slides.body_md: **Theorem.** The diagonals of a parallelogram **bisect each other**: $OA = OC$ and $OB = OD$.

visual.alt: Parallelogram A B C D with the diagonals A C and B D dashed. They cross at O. Tick marks show that O A equals O C and O B equals O D.
visual.caption: The diagonals bisect each other at O.

slides.narration: The diagonals of a parallelogram cross at a point O. The theorem says that O is the mid-point of both diagonals. The tick marks show that O A equals O C, and O B equals O D. In a parallelogram with A C equal to ten point eight six five one seven two and B D equal to seven point one zero two six seven nine, the half lengths are five point four three two five eight six and three point five five one three three nine. Now the proof.

slides.heading: Proof: the diagonals bisect each other
slides.body_md: Compare the shaded triangles $AOB$ and $COD$.

visual.alt: Table of five claims and reasons proving that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, by the congruent triangles A O B and C O D.

slides.narration: Compare the triangles A O B and C O D. A B equals C D, as opposite sides. The angles O A B and O C D are alternate angles, because A B is parallel to D C, so they are equal. The angles O B A and O D C are also alternate angles, so they are equal. Two angles and the included side agree, so the triangles are congruent. Hence O A equals O C and O B equals O D.

slides.heading: A diagonal makes two congruent triangles
slides.body_md: The diagonal $AC$ cuts the parallelogram into $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle CDA$. They are **congruent**, so they have **equal areas**: each is half of the parallelogram.

visual.alt: Parallelogram A B C D cut along the diagonal A C into two shaded triangles, A B C and C D A. The marked angles at A and C are equal alternate angles, and the diagonal A C is common to both triangles.
visual.caption: A diagonal cuts a parallelogram into two congruent triangles.

slides.narration: A diagonal cuts a parallelogram into two triangles. In the figure the triangles A B C and C D A are shaded. They share the diagonal A C, and the alternate angles at A and at C are equal. So the triangles are congruent. Congruent triangles have equal area, so each is half of the parallelogram. And the two diagonals together make four triangles at O, each with area one quarter, here seven point nine four six five two eight.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: the diagonals with x
slides.body_md: The diagonals of parallelogram $ABCD$ meet at $O$, with $OA = (3x - 1)$ cm, $OC = (x + 9)$ cm and $BD = 22$ cm. Find $x$, $AC$ and $OB$.

visual.alt: Parallelogram A B C D with the diagonals crossing at O. O A is three x minus one and O C is x plus nine. The diagonal B D is twenty two centimetres.
visual.caption: Diagonals bisect each other: find x, AC and OB.

slides.narration: The diagonals bisect each other, so O A equals O C. Three x minus one equals x plus nine, which gives two x equals ten, and x is five. Then O A and O C are fourteen each, and A C is twenty eight centimetres. For the other diagonal, B D is twenty two, and O is its mid-point, so O B is eleven centimetres.

slides.heading: Quick check: a ratio of angles
slides.body_md: Use the angle sum for neighbouring angles.

visual.alt: Parallelogram A B C D with angle A and angle C each sixty two degrees, shown with one arc, and angle B and angle D each one hundred eighteen degrees, shown with two arcs.
visual.caption: Opposite angles are equal; neighbouring angles add to 180 degrees.

slides.narration: The neighbouring angles of a parallelogram shaped dance floor are in the ratio seven to five. Find the smaller angle. Think about what the two angles add up to, then split that total in the given ratio.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a triangle at the centre
slides.body_md: In parallelogram $ABCD$, $AB = 9$ cm, $AC = 14$ cm and $BD = 11$ cm. Find the perimeter of $\triangle AOB$.

visual.alt: Table for triangle A O B in a parallelogram with A B nine, A C fourteen and B D eleven: O A is seven, O B is five point five and the perimeter is twenty one point five.

slides.narration: The sides of triangle A O B are A B, O A and O B. A B is nine centimetres. The diagonals bisect each other, so O A is half of fourteen, which is seven, and O B is half of eleven, which is five point five. The perimeter is nine plus seven plus five point five, which is twenty one point five centimetres. Notice that we never needed the other sides.

slides.heading: Summary of part 1
slides.body_md: Every result here comes from the **parallel sides**: co-interior and alternate angles, then congruent triangles.

rows: also gives a parallelogram; opposite angles equal
bisect each other; each cuts it into two congruent triangles

visual.alt: Summary table of part one: opposite sides, opposite angles, neighbouring angles, one equal and parallel pair, and the diagonals of a parallelogram.

slides.narration: Here is the summary of part one. In a parallelogram the opposite sides are equal and parallel, the opposite angles are equal, and neighbouring angles add to one hundred eighty degrees. One equal and parallel pair is enough to make a parallelogram. The diagonals bisect each other, and each diagonal cuts the parallelogram into two congruent triangles. Part two looks at special parallelograms.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Proof (3 marks):** the parallel lines and the angle relation 1 + the congruence or sum 1 + the conclusion 1
**Angles:** give the reason: opposite, co-interior or alternate
**Algebra:** form the equation from the **equal** pair, then check
**Mistake:** $\angle A = \angle B$ for neighbours; they add up to $180^\circ$

rows: the diagonals bisect each other; they are equal only in a rectangle
write the reason: alternate, co-interior, opposite sides
$\triangle ABC \cong \triangle CDA$ written without naming the condition
say angle side angle or side angle side

visual.alt: Table of four common slips of part one and their corrections: neighbouring angles add to one hundred eighty, the diagonals are equal only in a rectangle, every step needs a reason, and the congruence condition must be named.

slides.narration: Here is how marks are awarded. A three mark proof gives one mark for the parallel lines and the angle relation, one for the congruence or the angle sum, and one for the conclusion. Always write the reason beside each step. For algebra, form the equation from the pair that is equal, then check your answer. The two common mistakes are treating neighbouring angles as equal, and claiming the diagonals are equal.

decks.title: Rectilinear Figures: Parallelograms — Part 2: Rhombus, rectangle and square
goals: Describe the rhombus, rectangle and square as special parallelograms
Prove that the diagonals of a rhombus meet at right angles
Use the diagonal properties of rectangles and squares in problems
Identify a figure from the properties of its diagonals

slides.heading: Rhombus, rectangle and square
slides.body_md: Add one condition to a parallelogram and you get a **rhombus**, a **rectangle** or a **square**. Each keeps every parallelogram property and gains something about its **diagonals**.

visual.alt: Flow of four boxes: a parallelogram becomes a rhombus when all four sides are equal, and a rectangle when one angle is a right angle. A rhombus with a right angle, or a rectangle with equal sides, is a square.
visual.caption: The special parallelograms

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Start with a parallelogram. Make all four sides equal and you get a rhombus. Make one angle a right angle and you get a rectangle. Do both and you get a square. Each of these special parallelograms keeps every property from part one, and gains new facts about its diagonals. We prove one and use all of them.

slides.heading: The rhombus
slides.body_md: A **rhombus** is a parallelogram with **all four sides equal**. It has every property of a parallelogram: opposite angles equal and diagonals that bisect each other.

visual.alt: Rhombus A B C D. All four sides carry the same tick mark, so they are equal, and opposite sides carry matching arrow marks, so they are parallel.
visual.caption: A rhombus: a parallelogram with four equal sides.

slides.narration: A rhombus is a parallelogram with all four sides equal. The tick marks in the figure show the four equal sides, and the arrows show that opposite sides are parallel. A rhombus is a parallelogram first, so its opposite angles are equal, neighbouring angles add to one hundred eighty, and its diagonals bisect each other. The new fact is about the diagonals.

slides.heading: Diagonals of a rhombus
slides.body_md: **Theorem.** The diagonals of a rhombus meet at **right angles**, and each diagonal **bisects** the angles at its ends.

visual.alt: Rhombus A B C D with its diagonals dashed, crossing at O at a right angle marked by a small square. The tick marks show that O A equals O C and O B equals O D.
visual.caption: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles.

slides.narration: The diagonals of a rhombus cross at a right angle, marked by the small square. They also bisect each other, shown by the tick marks, and each diagonal bisects the angles at its ends. This makes four congruent right triangles at the centre. In the figure the diagonals are thirty two and twenty four centimetres, so the half lengths are sixteen and twelve, and every side is twenty.

slides.heading: Proof: which triangles to compare
slides.body_md: Compare $\triangle AOB$ and $\triangle AOD$ (shaded): $AB = AD$, $OB = OD$ and $AO$ is common.

visual.alt: Rhombus A B C D with triangles A O B and A O D shaded. A B equals A D, O B equals O D, and A O is common. The angles at O in the two triangles are marked m and are equal.
visual.caption: Triangles A O B and A O D match on three sides.

slides.narration: To prove that the diagonals are perpendicular, compare the shaded triangles A O B and A O D. The sides A B and A D are equal, because they are sides of a rhombus. O B equals O D, because the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other. And A O is common to both. So the three sides match, and the triangles are congruent.

slides.heading: Proof: the angles at O
slides.body_md: The matching angles at $O$ are equal, and they lie on a straight line.

rows: diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other

visual.alt: Table of seven claims and reasons proving that the diagonals of a rhombus meet at right angles, by the congruent triangles A O B and A O D.

slides.narration: Here is the full proof. The three pairs of sides are equal, so triangles A O B and A O D are congruent, side side side. Then the angles at O, A O B and A O D, are equal. But they lie on the straight line B D, so they add up to one hundred eighty degrees. Two equal angles with sum one hundred eighty must each be ninety degrees. So the diagonals meet at right angles.

slides.heading: Quick check: every rhombus
slides.body_md: Pick the property that holds for every rhombus.

visual.alt: Rhombus A B C D with its diagonals dashed, crossing at O at a right angle marked by a small square. The tick marks show that O A equals O C and O B equals O D.
visual.caption: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles.

slides.narration: Which statement holds for every rhombus, including a rhombus that is not a square? Think about the figure. Remember that equal diagonals and right angles at the corners belong only to the square. Look for the property proved on the last slide.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the side from the diagonals
slides.body_md: The diagonals of a rhombus are $48$ cm and $14$ cm. Find the length of a side and the perimeter.

visual.alt: Rhombus with diagonals forty eight centimetres and fourteen centimetres, drawn to scale, crossing at right angles at O. The side is to be found.
visual.caption: Drawn to scale: diagonals 48 cm and 14 cm.

slides.narration: The diagonals bisect each other at right angles, so the half lengths are twenty four and seven, and they form a right triangle with a side of the rhombus as hypotenuse. By Pythagoras, the side squared is five hundred seventy six plus forty nine, which is six hundred twenty five, so the side is twenty five centimetres. The perimeter is four times twenty five, which is one hundred centimetres.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: angles of a rhombus
slides.body_md: In rhombus $ABCD$, $\angle DAB = 76^\circ$. Find $\angle ABC$, $x = \angle BAC$ and $\angle ABD$.

visual.alt: Rhombus A B C D with angle D A B equal to seventy six degrees. Its diagonals are dashed and cross at O at a right angle. The angle B A C is marked x.
visual.caption: Rhombus with angle A = 76 degrees; find angle BAC and angle ABD.

slides.narration: Neighbouring angles add to one hundred eighty, so angle A B C is one hundred four degrees. The diagonal A C bisects the angle at A, so x is half of seventy six, which is thirty eight degrees. The diagonal B D bisects the angle at B, so angle A B D is half of one hundred four, which is fifty two degrees. Check: in the right triangle at O, thirty eight plus fifty two is ninety.

slides.heading: Quick check: a rhombus fill-in
slides.body_md: Find the perimeter from the two diagonals.

visual.alt: Table of four steps for a rhombus with diagonals forty eight and fourteen centimetres: the half-diagonals are twenty four and seven, the side is twenty five and the perimeter is one hundred centimetres.

slides.narration: A rhombus shaped brooch has diagonals of ten centimetres and twenty four centimetres. What is its perimeter? Follow the worked example: find half of each diagonal, use the right angle at the centre, then multiply the side by four.

slides.heading: The rectangle
slides.body_md: A **rectangle** is a parallelogram with **four right angles**. Its diagonals are **equal** and bisect each other, so $OA = OB = OC = OD$.

visual.alt: Rectangle A B C D with its equal diagonals dashed, crossing at O. The four half-diagonals O A, O B, O C and O D carry the same tick mark, so they are equal. The four corners are right angles.
visual.caption: The diagonals of a rectangle are equal and bisect each other.

slides.narration: A rectangle is a parallelogram with four right angles. Its diagonals are equal, and because they bisect each other, the four pieces from the centre O are all equal. In the figure the four tick marks show that O A, O B, O C and O D are equal. So the centre of a rectangle is the same distance from all four corners. Next, why the diagonals are equal.

slides.heading: Why the diagonals of a rectangle are equal
slides.body_md: Compare $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DCB$ on the common side $BC$.

visual.alt: Table of five claims and reasons proving that the diagonals of a rectangle are equal, by the congruent triangles A B C and D C B.

slides.narration: Compare the triangles A B C and D C B. A B equals D C, opposite sides. The angles at B and C are both right angles. And B C is common. Two sides and the angle between them agree, so the triangles are congruent, side angle side. So A C equals D B: the diagonals are equal. Notice that the right angle was needed. A general parallelogram does not have equal diagonals.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a rectangle with a diagonal
slides.body_md: A rectangle has length $24$ cm and diagonal $26$ cm. Find the breadth and the perimeter of $\triangle AOB$.

visual.alt: Rectangle A B C D drawn to scale with length A B equal to twenty four centimetres and the diagonal A C equal to twenty six centimetres. The breadth B C is to be found.
visual.caption: Drawn to scale: A B = 24 cm, A C = 26 cm.

slides.narration: In the right triangle A B C, the breadth squared is six hundred seventy six minus five hundred seventy six, which is one hundred, so the breadth is ten centimetres. The diagonals are equal and bisect each other, so O A and O B are each half of twenty six, which is thirteen. The perimeter of triangle A O B is twenty four plus thirteen plus thirteen, which is fifty centimetres.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: angles in a rectangle
slides.body_md: In rectangle $ABCD$, $\angle ADB = 28^\circ$. Find $y = \angle ABD$ and $z = \angle AOB$.

visual.alt: Rectangle A B C D with diagonals A C and B D crossing at O. The angle A D B is twenty eight degrees. The angle A B D is marked y and the angle A O B is marked z.
visual.caption: Rectangle with angle ADB = 28 degrees; find y = angle ABD and z = angle AOB.

slides.narration: The angle at A is a right angle, so in triangle A B D the angle y is ninety minus twenty eight, which is sixty two degrees. The diagonals are equal and bisect each other, so O A equals O B, and triangle A O B is isosceles with base angles sixty two. So z is one hundred eighty minus two times sixty two, which is fifty six degrees.

slides.heading: The square
slides.body_md: A **square** is both a rectangle and a rhombus: four equal sides and four right angles. Its diagonals are **equal**, meet at **right angles**, bisect each other, and make **45 degrees** with the sides.

visual.alt: Square A B C D with its diagonals dashed, crossing at O at a right angle. All four sides carry the same tick, and the four half-diagonals carry the same double tick. The diagonal A C makes forty five degrees with the side A B.
visual.caption: Square: equal diagonals that meet at right angles and bisect the corners.

slides.narration: A square is a rectangle and a rhombus at the same time. It has four equal sides and four right angles. Its diagonals are equal, like a rectangle, and meet at right angles, like a rhombus. They also bisect the corners, so each diagonal makes forty five degrees with the sides. The figure shows the forty five degree angle, the right angle at the centre, and the equal half diagonals.

slides.heading: Quick check: a square has both
slides.body_md: Decide whether a square has the properties of both families.

rows: Diagonals bisect each other and the corners

sections.heading: 1. Sides and angles of a parallelogram
sections.body_md:
A **parallelogram** $ABCD$ has $AB \parallel DC$ and $AD \parallel BC$. Then:

- **Opposite sides are equal:** $AB = DC$, $AD = BC$ (the proof is not in the ICSE 2028 Class IX syllabus; the result is used).
- **Opposite angles are equal:** $\angle A = \angle C$, $\angle B = \angle D$.
- **Neighbouring angles add up to $180^\circ$** (co-interior angles between parallel sides), and all four angles add up to $360^\circ$.

For $AB = 8$ cm, $AD = 4.5$ cm and $\angle A = 62^\circ$: $\angle B = 118^\circ$ and the perimeter is $25$ cm.

key_terms.definition_md: A quadrilateral whose opposite sides are parallel.
Two angles on the same side of a transversal between two parallel lines; they add up to 180 degrees.

formulas.latex: \angle A = \angle C, \quad \angle B = \angle D, \quad \angle A + \angle B = 180^\circ
formulas.label: Angles of a parallelogram

visual.alt: Parallelogram A B C D with angle A and angle C each sixty two degrees, shown with one arc, and angle B and angle D each one hundred eighteen degrees, shown with two arcs.
visual.caption: Opposite angles are equal; neighbouring angles add to 180 degrees.

sections.heading: 2. Proof that opposite angles are equal
sections.body_md:
**Proof.** In parallelogram $ABCD$, $AD \parallel BC$ with the transversal $AB$ gives $\angle A + \angle B = 180^\circ$. Also $AB \parallel DC$ with the transversal $BC$ gives $\angle B + \angle C = 180^\circ$. Hence $\angle A = \angle C$. In the same way $\angle B = \angle D$.

**From one equal and parallel pair.** If $AB \parallel DC$ and $AB = DC$ (a quadrilateral that is then a parallelogram; the proof of that test is not in the ICSE 2028 Class IX syllabus), join $AC$. Then $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle CDA$ (side angle side: $AB = CD$, $\angle BAC = \angle DCA$ alternate, $AC$ common). So $\angle B = \angle D$ and $\angle BCA = \angle DAC$, which are alternate angles, so $AD \parallel BC$. Adding, $\angle A = \angle BAC + \angle CAD = \angle DCA + \angle ACB = \angle C$.

key_terms.definition_md: Angles on opposite sides of a transversal between two parallel lines; they are equal.
Matching sides and angles of congruent triangles; they are equal.

sections.heading: 3. Diagonals of a parallelogram
sections.body_md:
The diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ meet at $O$.

- **They bisect each other:** $OA = OC$ and $OB = OD$.
- **Each diagonal divides the parallelogram into two congruent triangles:** $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle CDA$, so each has half the area.
- The two diagonals make four triangles at $O$ of **equal area**.

**Proof that the diagonals bisect each other.** In $\triangle AOB$ and $\triangle COD$: $AB = CD$, $\angle OAB = \angle OCD$ and $\angle OBA = \angle ODC$ (alternate angles, $AB \parallel DC$). So the triangles are congruent (angle side angle) and $OA = OC$, $OB = OD$.

**Proof that a diagonal gives congruent triangles.** In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle CDA$: $\angle BAC = \angle DCA$, $AC$ is common, $\angle BCA = \angle DAC$ (alternate angles): congruent (angle side angle).

For $AC = 28$ and $BD = 22$: $OA = 14$ and $OB = 11$.

key_terms.definition_md: A line segment joining two opposite corners of a quadrilateral.
To cut into two equal parts.

visual.alt: Parallelogram A B C D with the diagonals crossing at O. Triangles A O B and C O D are shaded. Their sides A B and C D carry the same tick marks. Angle O A B equals angle O C D, marked p, and angle A B O equals angle C D O, marked q.
visual.caption: Triangles A O B and C O D match: angle, side, angle.

sections.heading: 4. The rhombus
sections.body_md:
A **rhombus** is a parallelogram with **four equal sides**. Besides every parallelogram property, its diagonals:

- meet at **right angles**, and
- **bisect the angles** at their ends.

**Proof that the diagonals meet at right angles.** In $\triangle AOB$ and $\triangle AOD$: $AB = AD$, $OB = OD$ and $AO$ is common, so they are congruent (side side side). Hence $\angle AOB = \angle AOD$. These two angles lie on the straight line $BD$ and add up to $180^\circ$, so each is $90^\circ$.

**Using it.** The half-diagonals are the legs of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is a side: diagonals $48$ and $14$ give $\sqrt{24^2 + 7^2} = 25$ and a perimeter of $100$. For $\angle A = 76^\circ$: $\angle BAC = 38^\circ$ and $\angle ABD = 52^\circ$.

key_terms.definition_md: A parallelogram with all four sides equal.

visual.alt: Rhombus A B C D with triangles A O B and A O D shaded. A B equals A D, O B equals O D, and A O is common. The angles at O in the two triangles are marked m and are equal.
visual.caption: Triangles A O B and A O D match on three sides.

sections.heading: 5. The rectangle
sections.body_md:
A **rectangle** is a parallelogram with **four right angles**. Its diagonals are **equal**, so $OA = OB = OC = OD$.

**Proof.** In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DCB$: $AB = DC$, $\angle ABC = \angle DCB = 90^\circ$ and $BC$ is common, so they are congruent (side angle side) and $AC = DB$.

**Using it.** $AC^2 = AB^2 + BC^2$ (right angle at $B$). For $AB = 24$ and $AC = 26$: $BC = 10$, $OA = OB = 13$ and the perimeter of $\triangle AOB$ is $50$. If $\angle ADB = 28^\circ$, then $\angle ABD = 62^\circ$ and $\angle AOB = 180^\circ - 2 \times 62^\circ = 56^\circ$.

key_terms.definition_md: A parallelogram with four right angles.

visual.alt: Rectangle A B C D with its equal diagonals dashed, crossing at O. The four half-diagonals O A, O B, O C and O D carry the same tick mark, so they are equal. The four corners are right angles.
visual.caption: The diagonals of a rectangle are equal and bisect each other.

sections.heading: 6. The square and the family
sections.body_md:
A **square** is a rectangle and a rhombus: four equal sides, four right angles, **equal diagonals that meet at right angles**, bisect each other and make $45^\circ$ with the sides.

In a parallelogram, **perpendicular diagonals** give a rhombus (all four sides are equal) and **equal diagonals** give a rectangle; both together give a square.

For a square of diagonal $18$ cm: $OA = 9$ cm and the area is $2 \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times 18 \times 9 = 162$ cm$^{2}$.

key_terms.definition_md: A parallelogram that is both a rectangle and a rhombus.

sections.heading: 7. A routine for problems
sections.body_md:
1. **Draw** the figure and mark what is given.
2. **Name the family:** parallelogram, rhombus, rectangle or square.
3. **List the facts** it carries: angles ($A + B = 180^\circ$), diagonals (bisect; perpendicular; equal).
4. **Find a triangle at $O$** (or a triangle cut by a diagonal) and use the angle sum, Pythagoras or congruence.
5. **Write a reason** beside every step.

For equations in $x$, use the pair that is equal (opposite sides, opposite angles, $OA = OC$) and check the answer.

sections.heading: 8. Exam tips and common mistakes
sections.body_md:
**Mark split.** A 3-mark proof: the parallel lines and angle relation (1), the congruence or sum with its condition (1), the conclusion (1). A 10-mark structured question: part (a) is usually the proof, parts (b) and (c) use it with numbers.

**Common mistakes**
- Writing $\angle A = \angle B$ for neighbouring angles; they add up to $180^\circ$.
- Saying the diagonals of every parallelogram are equal; they are equal only in a rectangle (or square).
- Saying the diagonals of a rectangle meet at right angles; that is a rhombus fact.
- Using a whole diagonal as a leg of a right triangle instead of the half-diagonal.
- Forgetting to name the congruence condition (angle side angle, side angle side, side side side).
- Giving a proof without a reason beside each step.

key_terms.definition_md: Triangles with all matching sides and angles equal.

cards.front_md: What is a **parallelogram**?
cards.back_md: A quadrilateral in which both pairs of opposite sides are parallel.

cards.front_md: What are **co-interior angles**?
cards.back_md: Two angles on the same side of a transversal between parallel lines; they add up to $180^\circ$.

cards.front_md: What is a **rhombus**?
cards.back_md: A parallelogram with all four sides equal.

cards.front_md: What is a **rectangle**?
cards.back_md: A parallelogram with four right angles.

cards.front_md: What is a **square**?
cards.back_md: A parallelogram that is both a rectangle and a rhombus: four equal sides and four right angles.

cards.front_md: What does it mean to **bisect**?
cards.back_md: To cut into two equal parts.

cards.front_md: Angle rule for neighbouring angles of a parallelogram?
cards.back_md: $\angle A + \angle B = 180^\circ$.

cards.front_md: Angle rule for opposite angles of a parallelogram?
cards.back_md: $\angle A = \angle C$ and $\angle B = \angle D$.

cards.front_md: Rule for the diagonals of a parallelogram?
cards.back_md: $OA = OC = \dfrac{1}{2}AC$ and $OB = OD = \dfrac{1}{2}BD$.

cards.front_md: Relation for a rectangle with sides $l$, $b$ and diagonal $d$?
cards.back_md: $d^2 = l^2 + b^2$, and the diagonals are equal.

cards.front_md: Area of a square of diagonal $d$?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{d^2}{2}$: two triangles of base $d$ and height $\dfrac{d}{2}$.

cards.front_md: Why are the opposite angles of a parallelogram equal?
cards.back_md: $\angle A + \angle B = 180^\circ$ and $\angle B + \angle C = 180^\circ$ (co-interior angles), so $\angle A = \angle C$.

cards.front_md: How is the equal-opposite-angles result proved from one equal and parallel pair?
cards.back_md: Join $AC$: $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle CDA$ (side angle side), then add the angles at $A$ and $C$.

cards.front_md: Why do the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other?
cards.back_md: $\triangle AOB \cong \triangle COD$ (angle side angle: alternate angles and $AB = CD$), so $OA = OC$ and $OB = OD$.

cards.front_md: Why does a diagonal cut a parallelogram into congruent triangles?
cards.back_md: $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle CDA$: alternate angles at $A$ and $C$, and $AC$ common (angle side angle).

cards.front_md: Why do the diagonals of a rhombus meet at right angles?
cards.back_md: $\triangle AOB \cong \triangle AOD$ (side side side), so $\angle AOB = \angle AOD$; they lie on a straight line, so each is $90^\circ$.

cards.front_md: Why are the diagonals of a rectangle equal?
cards.back_md: $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DCB$ (side angle side: $AB = DC$, right angles, $BC$ common).

cards.front_md: Why is a square both a rectangle and a rhombus?
cards.back_md: It has four right angles (rectangle) and four equal sides (rhombus).

cards.front_md: In a parallelogram the diagonals meet at right angles. What is it?
cards.back_md: A rhombus (the congruent triangles at the centre give four equal sides).

cards.front_md: Which diagonal facts does a square have?
cards.back_md: Equal, perpendicular, bisecting each other, and $45^\circ$ with the sides.

cards.front_md: Two opposite angles of a parallelogram sum to?
cards.back_md: $2 \times \angle A$, for example $2 \times 62^\circ = 124^\circ$; the other two sum to $236^\circ$.

cards.front_md: How many triangles of equal area do the diagonals make?
cards.back_md: Four, each with one quarter of the area of the parallelogram.

cards.front_md: Which special parallelograms have equal diagonals?
cards.back_md: The rectangle and the square.

cards.front_md: Which special parallelograms have perpendicular diagonals?
cards.back_md: The rhombus and the square.

cards.back_md: $\angle Q = \angle S = 116^\circ$ and $\angle R = 64^\circ$.

cards.front_md: Worked: rhombus with diagonals $48$ and $14$. Find the side.
cards.back_md: $\sqrt{24^2 + 7^2} = 25$, so the perimeter is $100$.

cards.front_md: Worked: rectangle with length $24$ and diagonal $26$. Find the breadth.
Common slip with neighbouring angles?
cards.back_md: Writing $\angle A = \angle B$. They add up to $180^\circ$; it is the **opposite** angles that are equal.

cards.front_md: Common slip with diagonals?
cards.back_md: Saying the diagonals of every parallelogram, or of a rhombus, are equal. Equal diagonals: rectangle and square only.

questions.stem_md: In a parallelogram $ABCD$, which pair of angles must be equal?
questions.solution_md: The opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, so $\angle A = \angle C$ (and $\angle B = \angle D$). Neighbouring angles such as $\angle A$ and $\angle B$ add up to $180^\circ$; they are equal only when the parallelogram is a rectangle.

questions.stem_md: A window frame is a parallelogram $PQRS$ with $\angle P = 112^\circ$. The angle $\angle Q$ is
questions.solution_md: Neighbouring angles of a parallelogram are co-interior angles between parallel sides, so they add up to $180^\circ$: $\angle Q = 180^\circ - 112^\circ = 68^\circ$. The value $112^\circ$ would be the opposite angle $\angle R$.

questions.stem_md: A mosaic piece is cut as a parallelogram $ABCD$ with $\angle A = (4x + 8)^\circ$ and $\angle C = (6x - 22)^\circ$. The angle $\angle B$ is
questions.solution_md: Opposite angles are equal, so $4x + 8 = 6x - 22$, giving $x = 15$. Then $\angle A = \angle C = 68^\circ$ and $\angle B = 180^\circ - 68^\circ = 112^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: The wooden leaf of a garden gate is a parallelogram $ABCD$ with $AB = (3y + 4)$ dm, $CD = (7y - 12)$ dm and $AD = 9$ dm. Its perimeter is
questions.solution_md: Opposite sides are equal, so $3y + 4 = 7y - 12$ and $y = 4$. Then $AB = CD = 16$ dm, and the perimeter is $2(16 + 9) = 50$ dm. The value $41$ dm forgets one of the two sides of $9$ dm.

questions.stem_md: Two neighbouring angles of a parallelogram-shaped mirror frame are in the ratio $2 : 3$. The larger of them measures
questions.solution_md: Neighbouring angles add up to $180^\circ$. Splitting $180^\circ$ in the ratio $2 : 3$ gives $\dfrac{2}{5} \times 180^\circ = 72^\circ$ and $\dfrac{3}{5} \times 180^\circ = 108^\circ$. The larger angle is $108^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: In a quadrilateral $ABCD$, the side $AB$ is parallel to the side $DC$ and $AB = DC$. Which statement is certainly true?
questions.solution_md: A quadrilateral with one pair of opposite sides equal and parallel is a parallelogram, so its opposite angles are equal: $\angle A = \angle C$. The other three statements hold only for special parallelograms (rectangle, rhombus), not for every one.

questions.stem_md: The two cross-wires of a parallelogram-shaped paper lantern frame $PQRS$ meet at $M$, and $PM = 7.4$ cm. The wire $PR$ is
questions.solution_md: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so $M$ is the mid-point of $PR$ and $PR = 2 \times PM = 2 \times 7.4 = 14.8$ cm.

questions.stem_md: The crossing rods of a parallelogram-shaped signboard frame $ABCD$ meet at $O$, with $OA = (2x + 3)$ cm and $OC = (5x - 9)$ cm. The rod $AC$ is
questions.solution_md: The diagonals bisect each other, so $OA = OC$: $2x + 3 = 5x - 9$ and $x = 4$. Then $OA = 11$ cm and $AC = 2 \times 11 = 22$ cm.

questions.stem_md: A parallelogram-shaped flower bed $ABCD$ has $AB = 8.6$ m, $AC = 15.2$ m and $BD = 9.4$ m, the diagonals crossing at $O$. The perimeter of $\triangle AOB$ is
questions.solution_md: The diagonals bisect each other, so $AO = \dfrac{15.2}{2} = 7.6$ m and $BO = \dfrac{9.4}{2} = 4.7$ m. The perimeter of $\triangle AOB$ is $8.6 + 7.6 + 4.7 = 20.9$ m. The value $33.2$ m is $8.6 + 15.2 + 9.4$, which uses the whole diagonals.

questions.stem_md: A parallelogram-shaped sheet $ABCD$ of card, with no right angle, is cut along the diagonal $AC$. The two triangular pieces are
questions.solution_md: The diagonal $AC$ divides a parallelogram into two congruent triangles, $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle CDA$, so the pieces are congruent (and have the same area). They are right-angled or isosceles only for special parallelograms.

questions.stem_md: A cloth patch in the shape of a parallelogram $ABCD$ is cut along the diagonal $AC$, and the piece $ABC$ has area $36$ cm$^{2}$. The area of the whole patch is
questions.solution_md: The diagonal cuts the parallelogram into two congruent triangles, which have equal areas. So the area of $ABCD$ is $2 \times 36 = 72$ cm$^{2}$.

questions.stem_md: Which statement holds for every rhombus, including a rhombus that is not a square?

options.text_md: Each of its angles is a right angle.
Its opposite sides are not parallel.
Its diagonals meet at right angles.

questions.solution_md: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles. They are equal only in a square, the angles are right angles only in a square, and the opposite sides of any rhombus (a parallelogram) are parallel.

questions.stem_md: A diamond-shaped signboard is a rhombus with diagonals of $18$ dm and $24$ dm. Each side is
questions.solution_md: The diagonals bisect each other at right angles, so each side is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs $9$ dm and $12$ dm: $\sqrt{9^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{225} = 15$ dm.

questions.stem_md: A rhombus-shaped brooch $ABCD$ has $\angle ABC = 124^\circ$. The angle $\angle BAC$ that the diagonal $AC$ makes with the side $AB$ is
questions.solution_md: $\angle A = 180^\circ - 124^\circ = 56^\circ$, and the diagonal $AC$ bisects $\angle A$ in a rhombus. So $\angle BAC = 28^\circ$. (Check: $AB = BC$, so in $\triangle ABC$ the base angles are $\dfrac{180^\circ - 124^\circ}{2} = 28^\circ$.)

questions.stem_md: A rectangular school banner has a diagonal of $41$ dm and a breadth of $9$ dm. Its length is
questions.solution_md: The corners are right angles, so $\text{length}^2 + 9^2 = 41^2$, giving $\text{length}^2 = 1681 - 81 = 1600$ and length $= 40$ dm.

questions.stem_md: Two straight paths run from corner to corner of a rectangular lawn $ABCD$ and cross at $O$. If $OA = 6.5$ m, the path $BD$ is
questions.solution_md: The diagonals of a rectangle are equal and bisect each other, so $OA = OB = OC = OD = 6.5$ m and $BD = OB + OD = 13$ m.

questions.stem_md: The diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ of a rectangular plot $ABCD$ cross at $O$, and $\angle AOB = 70^\circ$. The angle $\angle OAB$ is
questions.solution_md: The diagonals of a rectangle are equal and bisect each other, so $OA = OB$ and $\triangle OAB$ is isosceles. Its base angles are $\dfrac{180^\circ - 70^\circ}{2} = 55^\circ$, so $\angle OAB = 55^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: A square cloth napkin has a diagonal of $14$ cm. Its area is
questions.solution_md: The diagonals of a square are equal, meet at right angles and bisect each other, so the diagonal $BD$ cuts the square into two triangles, each of base $14$ cm and height $7$ cm. The area is $2 \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times 14 \times 7 = 98$ cm$^{2}$.

questions.stem_md: A diagonal is drawn in a square. The angle it makes with a side of the square is
questions.solution_md: A diagonal of a square bisects the right angle at the corner, so it makes $\dfrac{90^\circ}{2} = 45^\circ$ with each side.

questions.stem_md: Which property does every rectangle have that a general parallelogram does not have?
questions.solution_md: In a rectangle the diagonals are equal. In a general parallelogram the diagonals are unequal, although they bisect each other, and opposite sides and opposite angles are equal in every parallelogram.

options.text_md: a rhombus that is not a square
a rectangle that is not a square
neither a rhombus nor a rectangle

questions.stem_md: The diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ of a parallelogram $ABCD$ meet at $O$. Which of these is not true for every parallelogram?

questions.stem_md: The diagonals of a parallelogram-shaped plot $ABCD$ meet at $O$. The area of $\triangle AOB$ is $(3x + 2)$ m$^{2}$ and the area of $\triangle COD$ is $(5x - 10)$ m$^{2}$. Find the area of the plot, in m$^{2}$.

$AD \parallel BC$, so $\angle BAD + \angle ABC = 180^\circ$ (co-interior angles): $\angle BAD = 180^\circ - 104^\circ = 76^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Recognise the parallelogram, then use the opposite angle and the co-interior angle.

The angles $\angle A$ and $\angle B$ are neighbouring angles, which are co-interior angles between the parallel sides $AD$ and $BC$, so they are not equal: they add up to $180^\circ$. It is the opposite angles ($\angle A$ and $\angle C$) that are equal.

questions.stem_md: $PQRS$ is a square whose diagonals meet at $O$. Find $\angle PRS$ and $\angle POQ$, with a reason for each.

A diagonal of a square bisects the right angle at the corner, so $\angle PRS = \dfrac{90^\circ}{2} = 45^\circ$.

The diagonals of a square meet at right angles, so $\angle POQ = 90^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: In the parallelogram $ABCD$, the sides satisfy $AD \parallel BC$ and $AB \parallel DC$. Use these two facts to prove that $\angle A = \angle C$ and $\angle B = \angle D$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$AD \parallel BC$ with the transversal $AB$: $\angle A + \angle B = 180^\circ$ (co-interior angles).

$AB \parallel DC$ with the transversal $BC$: $\angle B + \angle C = 180^\circ$ (co-interior angles).

So $\angle A + \angle B = \angle B + \angle C$, which gives $\angle A = \angle C$. In the same way, $\angle B + \angle C = 180^\circ = \angle C + \angle D$ gives $\angle B = \angle D$.

questions.solution_md: Two pairs of co-interior angles, each adding to $180^\circ$, share the angle $\angle B$ (and $\angle C$).

angle B + angle C = 180 (AB parallel to DC)
hence angle A = angle C, and in the same way angle B = angle D

questions.stem_md: The diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ of the parallelogram $ABCD$ cross at $O$. Show that $OA = OC$ and $OB = OD$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Compare $\triangle AOB$ and $\triangle COD$.

$AB = CD$ (opposite sides of a parallelogram). $\angle OAB = \angle OCD$ (alternate angles, $AB \parallel DC$, transversal $AC$) and $\angle OBA = \angle ODC$ (alternate angles, transversal $BD$).

So $\triangle AOB \cong \triangle COD$ (angle side angle). Hence $OA = OC$ and $OB = OD$ (corresponding parts), so the diagonals bisect each other.

answer.model_answer_md:
The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other, so $OB = OD$.

In $\triangle AOB$ and $\triangle AOD$: $AB = AD$ (sides of a rhombus), $OB = OD$ and $AO$ is common. So $\triangle AOB \cong \triangle AOD$ (side side side), and $\angle AOB = \angle AOD$.

These two angles lie on the straight line $BD$, so they add up to $180^\circ$. Each is $90^\circ$, so $AC \perp BD$.

questions.stem_md: In a rhombus-shaped kite $ABCD$, drawn by Kabir for a festival, $\angle DAB = 64^\circ$. Find $\angle ABC$, $\angle CAB$ and $\angle ABD$, giving a reason for each.

$\angle ABC = 180^\circ - 64^\circ = 116^\circ$ (neighbouring angles of a parallelogram add up to $180^\circ$).

The diagonal $AC$ bisects $\angle A$ in a rhombus, so $\angle CAB = \dfrac{64^\circ}{2} = 32^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: Explain why the two diagonals of a square are equal and meet at right angles, using what you know about the rectangle and the rhombus.

answer.model_answer_md:
A square is a rectangle (four right angles), and the diagonals of a rectangle are equal. So the diagonals of a square are equal.

A square is also a rhombus (four equal sides), and the diagonals of a rhombus meet at right angles.

So the diagonals of a square are equal and perpendicular, and they bisect each other because a square is a parallelogram.

questions.solution_md: A square belongs to both families, so it inherits the diagonal property of each.

a square is a rhombus, so its diagonals meet at right angles
a square is a parallelogram, so the diagonals bisect each other

questions.stem_md:
$ABCD$ is a parallelogram.

(a) Prove that $\angle A = \angle C$. [3]

(c) The parallelogram is a cloth patch with $AB = 9.5$ cm and $BC = 6.2$ cm. A tailor sews lace round all four edges at ₹ 3 per cm. Find the length of lace and its cost. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $AD \parallel BC$ with the transversal $AB$: $\angle A + \angle B = 180^\circ$ (co-interior angles). $AB \parallel DC$ with the transversal $BC$: $\angle B + \angle C = 180^\circ$. So $\angle A + \angle B = \angle B + \angle C$ and $\angle A = \angle C$.

(b) Opposite angles are equal: $3x + 12 = 5x - 28$, so $2x = 40$ and $x = 20$. Then $\angle A = \angle C = 72^\circ$ and $\angle B = \angle D = 180^\circ - 72^\circ = 108^\circ$.

(c) The opposite sides are equal, so $CD = 9.5$ cm and $AD = 6.2$ cm. The length of lace is the perimeter $2(9.5 + 6.2) = 2 \times 15.7 = 31.4$ cm. The cost is $31.4 \times 3 = $ ₹ 94.20.

questions.solution_md: Part (a) uses two pairs of co-interior angles; part (b) uses opposite angles equal and neighbouring angles supplementary; part (c) uses opposite sides equal for the perimeter.

questions.stem_md:
In a quadrilateral $ABCD$, $AB \parallel DC$ and $AB = DC$. The diagonal $AC$ is joined.

(a) Prove that $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle CDA$. [3]

(b) Hence prove that $\angle B = \angle D$ and that $AD \parallel BC$. [3]

(c) $AB = 8.4$ cm, $\angle ABC = 112^\circ$ and $\angle BAC = 38^\circ$. Find $\angle ACB$, $\angle DAC$ and $\angle BAD$, and state the length of $CD$. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle CDA$: $AB = CD$ (given); $\angle BAC = \angle DCA$ (alternate angles, $AB \parallel DC$, transversal $AC$); $AC$ is common. So $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle CDA$ (side angle side).

(b) By corresponding parts of congruent triangles, $\angle B = \angle D$ and $\angle BCA = \angle DAC$. The angles $\angle BCA$ and $\angle DAC$ are alternate angles for the lines $BC$ and $AD$ with the transversal $AC$, and they are equal, so $AD \parallel BC$. Thus $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.

(c) In $\triangle ABC$: $\angle ACB = 180^\circ - 112^\circ - 38^\circ = 30^\circ$. Then $\angle DAC = \angle ACB = 30^\circ$ (corresponding parts), and $\angle BAD = \angle BAC + \angle DAC = 38^\circ + 30^\circ = 68^\circ$. Also $CD = AB = 8.4$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Part (a) is the side-angle-side match from the alternate angles; part (b) reads off equal angles and then proves the second pair of sides parallel; part (c) is an angle sum in $\triangle ABC$ followed by the corresponding parts.

(a) AC common, so congruent (side angle side)
(b) angle BCA = angle DAC alternate, so AD parallel to BC

questions.stem_md:
The diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ of a parallelogram $ABCD$ meet at $O$.

(a) Prove that $OA = OC$ and $OB = OD$. [3]

(b) $AB = 10.8$ cm, $BC = 15.6$ cm, $AC = 24$ cm and $BD = 12$ cm. Find the perimeters of $\triangle AOB$ and $\triangle BOC$. [3]

(c) Find by how much the two perimeters differ, and explain why the difference equals $BC - AB$. Also explain why $\triangle AOB$ and $\triangle BOC$ have equal areas. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In $\triangle AOB$ and $\triangle COD$: $AB = CD$ (opposite sides); $\angle OAB = \angle OCD$ and $\angle OBA = \angle ODC$ (alternate angles, $AB \parallel DC$). So $\triangle AOB \cong \triangle COD$ (angle side angle) and $OA = OC$, $OB = OD$.

(b) $OA = \dfrac{24}{2} = 12$ cm and $OB = \dfrac{12}{2} = 6$ cm. The perimeter of $\triangle AOB$ is $10.8 + 12 + 6 = 28.8$ cm. As $OC = 12$ cm, the perimeter of $\triangle BOC$ is $15.6 + 12 + 6 = 33.6$ cm.

(c) The difference is $33.6 - 28.8 = 4.8$ cm. The triangles share the side $OB$ and have $OA = OC$, so the perimeters differ only in the third side: $BC - AB = 15.6 - 10.8 = 4.8$ cm.

The triangles $AOB$ and $BOC$ have equal bases $OA = OC$ on the line $AC$ and the same height, the perpendicular distance from $B$ to $AC$. So their areas are equal.

questions.solution_md: Part (a) is the angle-side-angle match; parts (b) and (c) use that the diagonals bisect each other, so each half-diagonal is shared or equal.

(a) triangles AOB and COD congruent (angle side angle)
(c) difference 4.8 = BC - AB (OB shared, OA = OC)
(c) equal areas: equal bases OA = OC, same height from B

The diagonals of a parallelogram $ABCD$ meet at $O$. A straight cut through $O$ meets $AB$ at $P$ and $DC$ at $Q$.

(c) $AB = 11$ cm, $AP = 4.1$ cm, $PQ = 8$ cm and $AD = 6$ cm. Find $CQ$, $DQ$ and the perimeter of the quadrilateral $APQD$. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In $\triangle AOP$ and $\triangle COQ$: $OA = OC$ (the diagonals bisect each other); $\angle AOP = \angle COQ$ (vertically opposite angles); $\angle OAP = \angle OCQ$ (alternate angles, $AB \parallel DC$, transversal $AC$). So $\triangle AOP \cong \triangle COQ$ (angle side angle), and $OP = OQ$.

questions.solution_md: The centre $O$ of the parallelogram makes the cut symmetric: the congruent triangles move the segment $AP$ across to $CQ$.

questions.stem_md:
$ABCD$ is a rhombus with diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ meeting at $O$.

(a) Prove that the diagonal $BD$ bisects $\angle ABC$ and $\angle ADC$. [3]

(b) If $\angle ABC = 116^\circ$, find $\angle ABD$, $\angle BAD$ and $\angle BAC$. [3]

(c) If $AC = 30$ cm and $BD = 16$ cm, find the length of a side, the perimeter, and the area of the rhombus. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In $\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle CBD$: $AB = CB$ and $AD = CD$ (sides of a rhombus), and $BD$ is common. So $\triangle ABD \cong \triangle CBD$ (side side side), and $\angle ABD = \angle CBD$, $\angle ADB = \angle CDB$. Thus $BD$ bisects $\angle ABC$ and $\angle ADC$.

(b) $\angle ABD = \dfrac{116^\circ}{2} = 58^\circ$. $\angle BAD = 180^\circ - 116^\circ = 64^\circ$ (co-interior angles), and $AC$ bisects $\angle A$, so $\angle BAC = \dfrac{64^\circ}{2} = 32^\circ$.

(c) The diagonals bisect each other at right angles: $OA = 15$ cm, $OB = 8$ cm. $AB^2 = 15^2 + 8^2 = 289$, so a side is $17$ cm and the perimeter is $4 \times 17 = 68$ cm. The rhombus is four right triangles with legs $15$ and $8$: area $= 4 \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times 15 \times 8 = 240$ cm$^{2}$.

questions.solution_md: Part (a) is a side-side-side match; part (b) uses the bisected angles; part (c) uses the right angle at $O$ and the four equal triangles.

(a) angle ABD = angle CBD and angle ADB = angle CDB

questions.stem_md:
$ABCD$ is a rectangle whose diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ meet at $O$.

(a) Prove that $AC = BD$. [3]

(b) Hence show that $OA = OB = OC = OD$. [3]

(c) $AB = 20$ cm and $BC = 21$ cm. Find $AC$, and the perimeters of $\triangle AOB$ and $\triangle BOC$. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DCB$: $AB = DC$ (opposite sides of a rectangle); $\angle ABC = \angle DCB = 90^\circ$; $BC$ is common. So $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DCB$ (side angle side) and $AC = DB$.

(b) A rectangle is a parallelogram, so its diagonals bisect each other: $OA = OC = \dfrac{1}{2}AC$ and $OB = OD = \dfrac{1}{2}BD$. Since $AC = BD$, all four are equal: $OA = OB = OC = OD$.

(c) In the right triangle $ABC$: $AC^2 = 20^2 + 21^2 = 400 + 441 = 841$, so $AC = 29$ cm. Then $OA = OB = 14.5$ cm. The perimeter of $\triangle AOB$ is $20 + 14.5 + 14.5 = 49$ cm. The perimeter of $\triangle BOC$ is $21 + 14.5 + 14.5 = 50$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Part (a) is a side-angle-side match using the right angles; part (b) combines it with the bisecting diagonals; part (c) uses the theorem of Pythagoras.

(a) BC common, congruent (side angle side), so AC = BD
(b) diagonals bisect each other: OA = OC = half of AC, OB = OD = half of BD
(b) AC = BD, so all four are equal
